sections.label: Content note
sections.body: **Content note:** this page discusses abuse, neglect, restraint and the deaths of people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. [Where to report abuse is listed below.](#kop-ri-report)

sections.label: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.heading: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
Group homes and other residential services for adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) are not part of the troubled teen industry, and Kids Over Profits does not track them. The people who live in them are adults, with a rights movement of their own led by self-advocates.

Disabled adults live where Medicaid pays a private company to house them, and private equity has bought many of those companies. Some of the same companies run youth programs, the same behavior control methods passed between the two, and residents of both are restrained, drugged and hurt in ways that too often go unreported.

We are not the experts on this system. The self-advocates and organizations listed below are.

sections.label: Housed where Medicaid pays
sections.heading: Housed where Medicaid pays
sections.body:
For more than a century disabled people were sent to institutions built to keep them apart. The first opened on Randall's Island in New York in 1847 and in Massachusetts in 1848, at the school later called the Fernald Center, whose administrators included eugenicists who called for disabled children to be kept apart. States sterilized people in their care: Indiana passed the first forced sterilization law in 1907, California sterilized more than 20,000 people, many of them adolescents in state care, and in *Buck v. Bell* (1927) the Supreme Court upheld the sterilization of Carrie Buck, a teenager held at the Virginia Colony for Epileptics and Feeble-Minded ([developmental disabilities and eugenics](/idd-timeline/)). The same institutions are among the roots of the troubled teen industry.

The state institutions held 194,650 people at their peak in 1967. Deinstitutionalization began in the 1960s, but underfunding left gaps that private providers filled, and from 1965 Medicaid let public money follow a person into a private placement ([the birth of the TTI](/birth-of-the-tti/)). Today most adults with IDD who get paid support live with family, Medicaid pays for nearly all of it, and private providers run almost every home outside a family's.

Table: Support for people with IDD, June 30, 2021
| Measure | Figure |
|---|---|
| People served by state developmental disability agencies | About 1.38 million[^1] |
| Living in a relative's home | 63 percent[^1] |
| Living in a group home, other group setting or intermediate care facility | About 299,000[^1] |
| Paid by Medicaid home and community-based services waivers, fiscal year 2021 | $47.1 billion, for 953,571 people[^1] |
| Paid for intermediate care facilities (ICF/IIDs), fiscal year 2021 | $8.68 billion, for 63,085 people[^1] |
| State-run facilities for 16 or more people | 106, with an average of 15,049 residents (194,650 in 1967)[^1] |
| Homes outside a family home, and how many states ran | About 232,000; 1,940 run by states[^1] |

sections.label: Bought by private equity
sections.heading: Bought by private equity
sections.body:
The providers were long mostly regional nonprofits and church groups. From 2013 to 2023 private equity firms made more than 1,000 acquisitions of disability and elder care providers,[^2] and they own two of the largest operators.

Sevita, formerly The MENTOR Network and Civitas Solutions, says it has 60,000 employees serving 70,000 people.[^3] Private equity has owned it since Madison Dearborn Partners bought it in 2001. Vestar Capital Partners followed in 2006 and took it public as Civitas Solutions in 2014 ([corporatization timeline](/corporatization/)), and Centerbridge Partners and The Vistria Group bought it in March 2019.[^4] In 2020 Senate Finance Committee reports on two of its affiliates found that REM Iowa had recurring critical incidents, including failures to report abuse or neglect,[^5] and that MENTOR Oregon showed "a consistent pattern of substandard care."[^6][^7]

BrightSpring Health Services, formerly ResCare, owned more than 600 residential facilities when the private equity firm KKR took control in March 2019. In seven states, KKR's facilities were 16 percent of the intermediate care facilities but received 40 percent of the most serious citations, more than 500, from March 2019 to the end of 2021. The company took out $1.1 billion in new loans and paid more than $135 million a year in interest. KKR and BrightSpring disputed the findings.[^8] BrightSpring filed to go public in January 2024.[^9]

sections.label: The same companies run youth programs
sections.heading: The same companies run youth programs
sections.body:
Several of these companies serve people on both sides of the age line, and disabled children placed in their youth programs can spend most of their childhood there: the Senate Finance Committee found Devereux stays of up to 6,928 days, almost 19 years, on its Florida campus.[^10]

Table: Companies in both systems
| Company | Adults with IDD | Youth programs |
|---|---|---|
| Sevita (The MENTOR Network) | 70,000 people served across its services[^3] | Foster care;[^3] NeuroRestorative's [14 group homes for young people in Illinois](/facility/neurorestorative-il/), in our records |
| BrightSpring (ResCare) | More than 600 residential facilities in 2019[^8] | Foster care and youth services;[^11] 2 West Virginia programs in our records |
| Devereux | More than 60 group homes in New Jersey,[^12] adult homes in Massachusetts[^13] | [43 programs in our records](/operator/devereux-advanced-behavioral-health/), 12 for children with IDD[^10] |
| AdvoServ (Bellwether) | 62 group homes in New Jersey until 2019[^14] | A Delaware program in our records |
| Judge Rotenberg Center | Adults[^15] | Children; [in our records](/facility/judge-rotenberg-educational-center-ma/) |

The records follow the companies across the line. ResCare's 2011 annual report called it the nation's largest private provider of services for people with developmental disabilities and described a youth division running residential treatment for young people with emotional and behavioral issues and for juveniles in the justice system, foster care, and 14 Job Corps centers.[^16] The Senate Finance Committee made The MENTOR Network the case study of its 2017 investigation of for-profit foster care,[^17] which raised concerns about treatment and deaths among foster children in its care,[^18] and in 2024 Florida moved to revoke NeuroRestorative's Florida license over its use of restraint and seclusion on children.[^19] AdvoServ, bought by Wellspring Capital Management in 2015,[^20] renamed itself Bellwether Behavioral Health in 2017 after ProPublica reported the deaths of three teenagers in its care and its frequent use of restraints;[^21] two years later New Jersey moved its adult group homes to other providers.[^14] Devereux began in 1912 as a small school in Pennsylvania and by 1983 was a national chain housing young people with IDD on Medicaid and public school money ([corporatization timeline](/corporatization/)).

sections.label: Controlled by force and drugs
sections.heading: Controlled by force and drugs
sections.body:
Much of the behavior control used in troubled teen programs was developed on disabled children. In 1965 Ivar Lovaas published his use of electric shock on autistic children at UCLA. Applied Behavior Analysis, defined in 1968, was first used to enforce compliance in disabled and autistic children, and in 1971 Matthew Israel founded the Behavior Research Institute, now the Judge Rotenberg Center ([experimental group psychology](/experimental-group-psychology/)). Point systems, levels and punishment for "noncompliance" passed back and forth between these programs and the ones built for troubled teens.

The Judge Rotenberg Center in Canton, Massachusetts, is the only facility in the country known to use electric skin shock on the people in its care, children and adults among them; the FDA estimated that about 50 people had treatment plans that included it.[^22] The FDA banned the devices in 2020. A federal appeals court vacated the ban in July 2021, Congress gave the FDA clear authority in 2022, and the FDA proposed a new ban in March 2024.[^23] As of October 2026 no final rule had been published.

Restraint kills here as it does in youth programs. In 1999 the GAO linked 24 deaths in one year to restraint or seclusion in facilities for people with mental illness or what was then called mental retardation, and found that federal rules covered restraint in ICFs and nursing homes but not in psychiatric hospitals, children's residential centers or community group homes.[^24] A 19-year-old autistic resident died after a restraint at Laurel Heights, a Universal Health Services youth hospital in Georgia.[^10]

Drugs are used the same way. Federal ICF/IID rules allow drugs to control behavior only as part of a plan to end the behavior, with team approval and a yearly attempt to withdraw them.[^25] Yet across many states in 2024-25, 37 percent of adults with IDD in group settings took medication for "behavioral challenges," and only 55 percent of them had a behavior plan.[^26]

sections.label: Harm that goes unreported
sections.heading: Harm that goes unreported
sections.body:
Group homes do not report most of what happens in them. HHS Inspector General audits from 2016 to 2018 found that group homes did not report 99 percent of critical incidents to investigators in Connecticut, 95 percent in Maine and 58 percent in Massachusetts, where one resident suffered head lacerations while aides restrained them.[^27] A 2018 joint report by the Inspector General, the Administration for Community Living and the Office for Civil Rights found media reports of health and safety problems in group homes in 49 states.[^28]

Reporters have found the deaths states missed. In 2016 the Chicago Tribune's "Suffering in Secret" found more than 1,300 cases of documented harm in Illinois group homes and their day programs since July 2011, and at least 42 deaths linked to abuse or neglect, far more than the state had reported.[^29] In 2011 The New York Times's "Abused and Used" found that New York kept workers who had physically or sexually abused residents of its homes and rarely reported abuse allegations to law enforcement;[^30] the state then changed how workers accused of abuse are disciplined.[^31]

sections.label: Where to report abuse
sections.heading: Where to report abuse
sections.body:
- **If someone is in danger now**, call 911.
- **Adult Protective Services** takes reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of adults with disabilities in most states. In some states a separate agency handles adults with developmental disabilities, or adults under 60. The National Adult Protective Services Association keeps [the reporting contact for every state and territory](https://www.napsa-now.org/help-in-your-area/).
- **The Eldercare Locator**, run by the federal government, refers callers to local agencies, mainly for older adults: call or text 1-800-677-1116, or visit [eldercare.acl.gov](https://eldercare.acl.gov/).
- **Protection and Advocacy agencies** are independent disability rights agencies in every state and territory. Find yours in the [National Disability Rights Network directory](https://www.ndrn.org/about/ndrn-member-agencies/).
- **Medicaid Fraud Control Units** investigate abuse and neglect of residents of health care facilities and board and care facilities, and of Medicaid enrollees in other settings ([HHS Office of Inspector General](https://oig.hhs.gov/fraud/medicaid-fraud-control-units-mfcu/)).
- Also tell the state agency that licenses the home or pays for the services.
- **988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline**, 24 hours: call or text [988](tel:988).

Our [reporting directory](/report-abuse/) lists agencies state by state.

sections.label: Organizations to learn from
sections.heading: Learn from the people who work on this
sections.body:
- [Self Advocates Becoming Empowered (SABE)](https://www.sabeusa.org/): The nationwide organization of self-advocates, people with intellectual and developmental disabilities speaking for themselves. Its priorities include closing institutions.
- [Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN)](https://autisticadvocacy.org/about-asan/): A national disability rights organization run by and for autistic people.
- [ADAPT](https://adapt.org/): A grassroots disability rights group known for direct action for the right to live at home, not in nursing homes and institutions.
- [National Disability Rights Network (NDRN)](https://www.ndrn.org/about/): The membership organization for the Protection and Advocacy agencies and Client Assistance Programs in every state and territory.
- [The Arc of the United States](https://thearc.org/about-us/): Has advocated for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities and their families since 1950, with chapters across the country.
- [National Council on Independent Living (NCIL)](https://www.ncil.org/about/): A cross-disability organization advocating for independent living and disability rights since 1982.

sections.label: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.heading: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.body: If you live or work in this system, or you are a self-advocate or a family member, and something on this page is wrong, please [tell us](/contact/). We will correct it.

sections.body: Figures checked against their sources on October 8, 2026.
